title: Share a bounded iterative divider in execute
motivation:
The bench retest reached 5.442 MHz median Fmax. Its 199.837 ns,
156-cell worst path crosses forwarding, EX, and the ALU. The four
full-width combinational DIV/REM expressions are the likely source
of most of that depth. A baseline RVFI trace at the canonical 2K,
-O3, ten-iteration settings with both bus stalls enabled saw two
DIV/REM retirements in the full run and zero within the 4,491,485
marked cycles. A shorter clock period should therefore raise marked
iterations per second with no direct divider stalls in that window.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU with a single shared 32-bit restoring
divider local to EX. Capture the forwarded source values and sign
controls at launch, with unsigned magnitudes and widened divisor
multiples D, 2D, and 3D. Produce two radix-4 digits per cycle. Each
digit subtracts the three multiples from the shifted partial dividend
in parallel using 35-bit trial differences. Select the largest multiple
with a nonnegative difference, using digit zero if all three borrow.
Divide work spans eight cycles after launch. On the last step, select
quotient or remainder, apply quotient sign from both operands or
remainder sign from the dividend, and send the result through the
existing EX/MEM register. Return all ones for divide by zero, the
original dividend for remainder by zero, and the RV32M-defined
INT_MIN/-1 results.

Advance the divide into EX/MEM by the ninth EX cycle on a ready bus,
including launch. This leaves one cycle for a load-use bubble or a
taken redirect within the existing ten-cycle successor-retirement window.
Hold the fetch PC and ID/EX until completion. Honor an older stalled
memory operation before launch, let older operations drain while
the divide runs, and inject side-effect-free EX/MEM bubbles until
the divide result is accepted. Retain a completed result while EX/MEM
is blocked and clear pending work on reset. Forward the result through
EX/MEM as for other ALU results and report the captured source values
in the single normal RVFI retirement. Keep the divider handshake
and cycle count in RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS, using the existing alternative
result formulas on the captured operands. Base integer and multiply
operations keep their current latency.

At the baseline cycle count, a median Fmax of 8.163 MHz would yield
18.18 iter/sec, a 50% gain. Compare the measured Gowin median Fmax and
worst path against the retest and remeasure marker cycles, since
pre-marker divides can shift the phase of the bus stalls. The 4.6%
acceptance hurdle is about 12.68 iter/sec.

implementation_notes:
# Shared iterative divider in EX

## Implementation

- The four RV32M divide and remainder operations share one restoring divider. Launch captures the forwarded operands, unsigned magnitudes, divisor multiples and result sign. Two radix-4 digits are computed in each of eight work cycles. Each digit tests `D`, `2D` and `3D` in parallel using 35-bit differences. A widened shift supplies `2D` from the registered divisor.
- EX advances a ready result on the ninth cycle including launch. Fetch and ID/EX hold while the divider runs, and EX/MEM receives bubbles with all side-effect controls cleared. An older stalled memory operation blocks launch. A result that cannot advance on the last step is latched until accepted. Reset clears pending work.
- The original instruction remains in ID/EX. Its captured forwarded operands travel with the result through EX/MEM to the single RVFI retirement. Consumers use the existing EX/MEM forwarding path. Base ALU and multiply operations retain their one-cycle EX latency.
- The recurrence yields an all-ones quotient and the original dividend as remainder when the divisor is zero. Quotient negation is disabled in that case. Unsigned magnitude arithmetic also produces the required `INT_MIN / -1` and `INT_MIN % -1` results. ALTOPS uses the original formulas on the captured operands with the same handshake and latency.
- Divider vectors moved to `test_divider.py` so they exercise the production divider independently of the combinational ALU. A guarded declaration include in `core.sv` lets the requested alphabetical Verilator glob lint successfully.

## Verification

- Verilator `-Wall` lint passed in both production and ALTOPS builds.
- Local `formal/run_all.sh` passed all 53 checks on the first attempt using the single-channel ALTOPS configuration, including `liveness_ch0`. Real arithmetic was checked with 1,112 divider vectors and the ISS cosimulation. The divider tests also exercised reset and result retention with a blocked response.
- All six cocotb runners passed. Pipeline tests confirmed a ten-cycle retirement gap for load-to-divide and taken-branch-to-divide, one-cycle forwarding to an immediate ALU consumer, and a single divide retirement after an older stalled store.
- Local cosimulation passed for selftest and all three random ELFs both with and without bus stalls. The canonical 2K, `-O3`, ten-iteration CoreMark run with both stalls enabled passed CRC and UART validation. Start was cycle 15,801 and stop was cycle 4,507,286.

## Gowin timing and CoreMark fitness

| Metric | Baseline retest | Shared divider |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Fmax across placement options 0, 1 and 2 (MHz) | 5.140 / 5.442 / 5.442 | 44.132 / 43.841 / 43.841 |
| Median Fmax (MHz) | 5.442 | 43.841 |
| Worst path arrival, placement option 0 (ns) | 199.837 | 27.953 |
| Worst path cells, placement option 0 | 156 | 38 |
| Logic cells | 12,312 | 2,818 |
| Registers | 460 | 628 |
| Marked CoreMark cycles | 4,491,485 | 4,491,485 |
| CoreMark iterations per second | 12.12 | 97.61 |

The option-0 worst path goes from the register file to ID/EX through ID, EX, IF and the hazard unit. Options 1 and 2 report a 28.104 ns worst path from MEM/WB through forwarding and the same front-end logic. The measured score exceeds the 12.68 iterations-per-second hurdle.
lesson: - 2026-11-19 hyp-20261119-001-r1s0 (regression, +705.36%): A shared nine-cycle EX divider removed combinational DIV/REM from the critical path, raising median Fmax from 5.442 to 43.841 MHz while preserving the marked CoreMark cycle count because the timed window had no DIV/REM retirements.

title: Move division and remainder into a shared multicycle execute unit
motivation:
Bench's 5.442 MHz baseline has a 199.837 ns, 156-cell worst path through
forwarding and the execute ALU. The ALU's signed and unsigned division and
remainder operators can put a full-width divider behind forwarding and ahead of
the shared EX/MEM result register. That path limits the clock for all instructions.
The unchanged CoreMark simulation with both buses stalled reproduced the logged
4,491,485 marker-bracketed cycles and canonical CRCs. Its retirement trace had
zero DIV/REM instructions inside the markers, one DIVU before, and one after.

hypothesis.motivation:

The unchanged CoreMark simulation with both buses stalled reproduced the logged

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Replace the combinational DIV, DIVU, REM, and REMU operators with one registered,
blocking execute unit that computes quotient and remainder together. On launch,
register the forwarded operand magnitudes, divisor multiples D, 2D, and 3D,
result sign, and operation. Process a zero-padded 36-bit dividend in six cycles,
taking three radix-4 digits per cycle. Each digit compares the shifted partial
remainder with the three multiples in parallel and selects the trial difference
for the largest fitting multiple. Select and sign-correct the registered magnitude
on completion, preserving RV32M divide-by-zero and signed-overflow results. This
limits each iterative clock path to three restoring digit steps.

Hold the DIV/REM instruction in EX and stop younger issue while older instructions
drain. Launch once when the older MEM entry can advance, inject EX/MEM bubbles
during the wait, and transfer the completed instruction once through the usual
forwarding and retirement path. Base ALU and multiply operations keep their
existing latency. One launch cycle and six digit cycles add seven cycles per
division, leaving at most nine cycles between successive retirements in the
zero-wait formal model, including an intervening redirect or load-use bubble.
Use the same launch, wait, and completion schedule with the existing ALTOPS
formulas so formal exercises the same interlocks and forwarding.

The baseline trace predicts zero direct divider stalls in the scored window.
The setup division can shift the pseudo-random stall sequence at
the start marker, so measure cycles again along with median Gowin Fmax. Check
whether the worst path moves off the original forwarding-to-ALU cone. With
unchanged cycles, 5.693 MHz clears the acceptance threshold and 8.163 MHz gives
the forecast 50 percent fitness gain.

changes.description: Implement the shared radix-4 quotient and remainder datapath and a fixed six-cycle iteration after launch. Subtract zero-extended 34-bit operands to get an explicit borrow bit and hold the completed result until accepted. Keep the DIV/REM ALTOPS constants and arithmetic under the same transaction timing.
Move all four divide and remainder operations into the divider and retain the combinational base ALU and all four multiplier operations.

Launch from valid decoded DIV/REM with fully forwarded sources. Latch the raw source values for RVFI at launch. Bubble EX/MEM until the result is ready, then send the original instruction metadata and result through EX/MEM once. Clear the divider and its in-flight state on reset.
Connect the divider wait to the issue interlock and preserve the existing single-channel RVFI and memory interfaces.

Hold the fetch PC and ID/EX payload during DIV/REM wait, independently of the MEM/WB advance control. Give an older stalled memory request priority over both divider launch and EX/MEM updates. Resume issue on result acceptance.

title: Predict taken control transfers with a tagged fetch BTB
motivation:
The bench core fetches PC+4 until EX redirects, so every taken branch and
jump discards the next fetch slot. Repeated CoreMark loop branches, calls,
and returns can reuse targets learned at the same instruction address.
The reported baseline critical path runs through the EX ALU, so the BTB
lookup should run in parallel with instruction-memory access from the
registered fetch PC.

hypothesis.motivation:
The bench core fetches PC+4 until EX redirects, so every taken branch and
jump discards the next fetch slot. Repeated CoreMark loop branches, calls,
and returns can reuse targets learned at the same instruction address.
The reported baseline critical path runs through the EX ALU, so the BTB
lookup should run in parallel with instruction-memory access from the
registered fetch PC.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Add a 32-entry direct-mapped branch target buffer indexed by PC[6:2].
Within the aligned 1 MiB instruction window, use PC[19:7] as the tag and
store the aligned target as bits [19:2]. Require an aligned in-range fetch
PC for lookup and aligned in-range source and target PCs for writes. On a
valid tag hit, use the stored target if the entry describes a jump or its
conditional counter predicts taken. Otherwise use PC+4. Learn eligible JAL
and JALR targets and allocate a conditional entry weakly taken on its first
taken outcome. Saturate the counter in matching conditional entries on both
outcomes. Use separate synchronously written tag, target and state arrays
with a common write enable. Read tags and state combinationally at the fetch
and update indices, and read the target at the fetch index. Reset only the
valid bits to keep the payload eligible for distributed RAM inference.

Advance to the predicted successor only when the fetch is accepted by ID.
With the combinational IF/ID bundle, the registered fetch PC itself is the
predicted successor of the valid instruction held in EX. Compare it with
the resolved architectural successor for every valid EX instruction to
recover from direction misses, changed indirect targets, and stale hits on
non-branches.
On mismatch, reload the resolved PC and squash the current IF/ID slot even
when imem is unavailable. During an older dmem stall, hold the fetch PC and
EX instruction and defer recovery and training until EX advances. Retain the
existing trap handling and report the resolved successor in RVFI.

With the evaluator's bus-ready sequence, a retirement-trace replay showed
that 64 entries save only about 5,000 more cycles than 32. The 32-entry RTL
prototype completed the canonical CoreMark run in 4,191,341 cycles versus
4,491,485 at baseline, with matching CRCs. Its Gowin placement results were
5.282, 5.628, and 5.628 MHz, giving 13.43 iterations/sec at the median and
a 10.8% gain over 12.12. The expected gain is 7% at baseline Fmax, with
about 5.314 MHz required to clear the acceptance threshold at those cycles.
The prototype used 12,869 LUT4s versus 12,312 at baseline and passed all 53
single-retire ALTOPS formal checks plus the fixture's RVFI cosim programs.

changes.description: Use the BTB prediction for accepted fetches and prioritize EX recovery over instruction-memory and load-use stalls.

Implement the 32-entry tagged target and counter table. Use the current matching counter at update time so consecutive loop iterations train correctly, including simultaneous lookup and update of one slot.

Resolve and report the architectural next PC, compare it against the current fetch PC, and emit one training event for each eligible valid control transfer that advances. Keep misaligned target traps and jump link results intact.
Wire lookup and training between IF, EX, and the table, and route the misprediction signal through the existing flush controls.
Keep older dmem holds ahead of recovery, squash on a qualified misprediction, and preserve independent imem and load-use behavior.

Add branch_target_buffer.sv to the runner's source list. Exercise warm taken loops and loop exits, a JALR whose target changes, a stale hit at a PC now holding a non-control instruction, and misaligned targets. Cover recovery with imem unavailable or an older dmem access stalled. Check bubble-free correct predictions, retired PCs and that wrong-path stores never issue.

lesson: - 2026-11-19 hyp-20261119-003-r1s2 (regression, +6.44%): With median Gowin Fmax still limited to 5.408 MHz by the forwarding-to-EX ALU path, the 32-entry fetch BTB's 6.7% CoreMark cycle savings yielded 12.90 iterations/s, below the 102.12 achieved by moving DIV/REM off that path in the same round.
